historical_growth.growth_divergence_warning: FLAGGED: Revenue 3yr CAGR (47.9%) diverges 71% from Equity 3yr CAGR (13.7%). All headline CAGRs are dominated by inorganic acquisitions (EastMed/DFM in FY23, Hub Aged Care in FY24, ARC Health and Cicada Health in FY26). These are not repeatable at the same rate. Organic ARC patient growth was ~3.7% in H1 FY26. Selected base growth of 10% reflects organic revenue growth (~5-8%) plus modest continuing bolt-on contribution, declining toward terminal 3%.
historical_growth.organic_growth_note: Organic ARC revenue growth estimated at 5-8% p.a.: ~3.7% enrolled patient growth (H1 FY26 organic) + capitation uplift (9.69% effective FY26, future formula reweighting positive). Through-cycle organic estimate 6-8%. Bolt-on acquisitions add 2-4pp in active years at low multiples. Base growth of 10% for Y1 is supportable but decelerates materially.
historical_growth.fcf_normalisation_note: FY25 FCF of $3,549k at 18.6% FCF margin is near a recent peak following margin expansion. H1 FY26 FCF annualised implies ~$2,760k (13.0% margin, partly seasonal). Normalised FCF anchored at $3,200k (FY26E estimate, ~15% FCF margin on ~$21.5M revenue), representing mid-cycle between FY25 peak and H1 FY26 run-rate. This is the appropriate base to avoid peak-FCF extrapolation.

wacc_rationale: Base WACC of 14.5% constructed from: NZ small-cap base rate 11.5% (midpoint of 11-12% NZ small-cap range) plus structural risk premiums: (1) +1.0% single-payer funding concentration — 100% of revenue ultimately flows from Health NZ/PHOs, which is under Commissioner control and fiscal pressure; (2) +0.5% clinical workforce constraint — GP shortage is structural and limits growth ceiling; (3) +1.0% micro-cap illiquidity — market cap ~NZD 44M, well below $300M threshold, thin NZX trading volumes; (4) +0.5% acquisition integration complexity — four acquisitions in 18 months, minority structures (67-80% owned subsidiaries), EastMed loss-making at NCI level. Total: 14.5%. Bull case uses 13.0% (assuming partial risk reduction from capitation formula success and M&A outperformance). Bear case uses 16.0% (escalated for funding or workforce deterioration).
valuation_philosophy: TAH.NZ is a micro-cap NZX healthcare compounder in a genuinely attractive niche (ARC medical services for an ageing NZ population). Revenue growth has been spectacular but almost entirely acquisition-driven. A disciplined DCF must strip out inorganic noise and model sustainable organic growth plus a conservative allowance for continuing bolt-on M&A. The high WACC (14.5% base) is justified by single-payer concentration, micro-cap illiquidity, and structural workforce constraints. FCF is anchored at FY26E normalised ~$3.2M rather than FY25 peak $3.55M to avoid extrapolating a margin peak. Terminal growth of 3% reflects NZ demographic tailwinds moderating over a very long horizon. The business does NOT need to assume 47% revenue growth — at normalised organic 5-10% growth with high FCF conversion, the DCF produces a defensible and internally consistent result.

base.description: Organic ARC growth ~7-8% plus modest bolt-on M&A contribution (~2pp), decelerating as market share matures and FY27 difficult backdrop materialises. FCF margin 15% (normalised, between FY25 peak 18.6% and H1 FY26 run-rate 13%). Terminal growth 3% reflecting multi-decade NZ demographic tailwind at maturity.

bull.description: ARC capitation formula reweighting from July 2026 materially increases revenue per enrolled patient. Successful ARC Health and Cicada Health integration drives faster Canterbury/BOP growth. NP Development Programme graduates expand capacity constraint. Digital Clinical Portal drives operating leverage to 17% FCF margin. One to two additional bolt-on acquisitions per year at TAH's demonstrated low entry multiples. Some risk premium compression as business scales toward $50M+ revenue.

bear.description: Health NZ funding constraint constrains or freezes capitation rates post FY26 uplift. GP enrolled patient attrition continues, dragging community GP segment into losses. Clinical workforce shortage constrains ARC expansion to near-zero organic growth. EastMed goodwill impairment materialises. Wage inflation for GPs and NPs compresses FCF margin to 13% (H1 FY26 run-rate). No further acquisitions. Small-cap risk premium rises as macro tightens.

sensitivity.matrix_note: Rows = WACC (ascending), Columns = Terminal Growth (ascending). Base case is row 4, col 3 ($3.46). All values in NZD per share using base FCF of $3,200k and growth rates [10%, 9%, 7%, 5%, 4%].

sanity_check.result: PASS. Base case IV of $3.46 implies EV/EBITDA of 6.3x (within hist. range 4.9x-12.7x), P/E of 11.1x (within hist. range 10.8x-30.5x), P/Sales of 1.6x (within hist. range 0.99x-3.90x). All implied multiples are internally consistent with historical trading ranges. Current market price of $4.40 implies 14.1x P/E and 8.0x EV/EBITDA — modestly above the base-case fair value, suggesting the stock is trading at approximately 27% premium to base-case DCF intrinsic value, though within the bull-case range.
key_observations: All historical CAGRs are acquisition-distorted and cannot be used directly. Custom organic growth estimate applied.
FY23 P/E of 30.5x was an acquisition-cost distortion (DFM/EastMed deal costs). Not representative of steady-state.
FY24 P/Sales of 0.99x was anomalously low (market did not price in the DFM/EastMed revenue addition properly).
High structural WACC of 14.5% is the key driver pulling base IV below current price. This is intentional and defensible given the micro-cap, single-payer, workforce-constrained risk profile.
Stock needs to trade above $4.98 (the base IV at WACC 13%, terminal 3%) to be 'fairly valued' under optimistic but realistic assumptions.

investment_summary.conclusion: At $4.40, TAH.NZ trades at a ~27% premium to base-case intrinsic value ($3.46) and is approximately at fair value under the bull case ($4.83). The stock is NOT cheap on a pure DCF basis at current price; it is priced for continued execution. The investment thesis requires faith in: (1) the new capitation formula delivering material revenue uplift per enrolled patient from July 2026; (2) the ARC segment continuing to grow organically despite workforce constraints; (3) management executing additional bolt-on acquisitions at historically low multiples. The bear case of $2.51 (down 43%) is plausible if Health NZ funding freezes or GP attrition accelerates. Risk-adjusted, the stock appears roughly fairly valued to slightly expensive at $4.40. An investor seeking 15% CAGR returns would need a $2.01 entry price against the base case terminal value — significantly below current levels. The stock is best suited to patient investors who believe in the long-duration NZ demographic tailwind and trust management's Kaizen-driven compounding philosophy, accepting the near-term difficult backdrop as a temporary obstacle rather than a structural impairment.
